name: Banana Grotesk
classification_notes: Low-contrast geometric grotesque with wide proportions. Conceived as a sketch of Akzidenz Grotesk from memory, with Gill Facia influencing the organic terminals. Distinctive banana-curve tails on 'a', 'g', 'f', 'j' and 't' give it a playful character without fully crossing into display territory.
designer: Meg Donohoe, Mitch Paone, Sebastian Carewe et al.
summary: A low-contrast geometric grotesque with wide proportions and organic banana-curve terminals, spanning seven weights with matching italics.
description: Banana Grotesk was developed over three years by the MNKY Type collective, beginning as a from-memory sketch of Akzidenz Grotesk refined through Gill Facia influences. The result is a wide-set sans-serif with swooping terminals on 'a', 'g', 'f', 'j' and 't' that add personality without tipping into novelty. It holds up across scales – from brand identities to editorial text – and pairs well with serif workhorses.
foundry_blurb: MNKY Type is an independent foundry split between New York and Chamonix, France, built around a team of designers from studios across the US and Europe. The studio runs straightforward size-based licensing and donates a portion of proceeds to animal sanctuaries and shelters. All typeface names must be monkey-related references.

name: Banana Mono
classification_notes: Monospace grotesque companion to Banana Grotesk. Shares the same curved humanist-inflected letterforms derived from Akzidenz-Grotesk sketched from memory, with Gill Facia characteristics visible particularly in the a, g, and f. Weights are precisely matched to the proportional family across all seven cuts.
summary: The monospace companion to Banana Grotesk, with seven matched weights and italics carrying its curved grotesque character into fixed-width territory.
description: Banana Mono carries the warmth of Banana Grotesk into fixed-width formats, with weights and proportions aligned across both families for consistent pairing. The design traces back to Mitch Paone sketching Akzidenz-Grotesk from memory, with Gill Facia's character folded in, most visible in the a, g, and f. Seven weights from Extralight to Extrabold, each with a matching italic, make it viable standalone for editorial or coding work as well as within brand systems.
foundry_blurb: Banana Mono takes the style of its proportional sibling into the monospace domain. With the same characteristic curves in all the right places, it works in harmony with Banana Grotesk, with weights precisely matched between the two families.

name: Elsa
classification_notes: High-contrast Didone serif drawing directly from Walbaum and Bodoni, with a first sketch dating to around 2018. The design departs from a straight Walbaum revival to pull in Didot and Bodoni details alongside early-twentieth-century references including Columbia-Antigua and Berthold's Augustea. Sturdy serifs carry the romans; the italics are markedly expressive.
summary: A confident Didone serif from MNKY Type's New York–Chamonix studio, drawing on Walbaum and Bodoni with sturdy romans and notably flamboyant italics aimed at decorative editorial work.
description: Elsa is a high-contrast serif in the Didone tradition, developed over several years from an initial Walbaum study into something that also absorbs Bodoni, Didot and early-twentieth-century references such as Columbia-Antigua. Four roman weights read with composure at text sizes, while the italics are drawn with enough ornamentation to hold their own as display cuts. It suits editorial and branding contexts where classical authority and some decorative flair are both wanted.
foundry_blurb: MNKY Type is an independent type foundry split between New York and Chamonix, France, offering retail and custom typefaces made with a broad network of collaborators. The foundry takes a contemporary approach to licensing and donates a portion of its proceeds to animal sanctuaries and shelters.

name: Albert
classification_notes: Extended geometric grotesque with retro-futurist character. Wide, chunky letterforms draw on Eurostile's proportions but are reworked with softer, more curvaceous contours. 18 styles across nine weights (Thin to Black) each with a companion italic. Basic Latin coverage only.
summary: A wide geometric grotesque that takes Eurostile's confident proportions as its starting point, then softens the angles into something more curvaceous across nine weights with matching italics.
description: Albert is an extended geometric grotesque built on Eurostile's wide, assertive proportions, reworked with softer curves and a more forward-looking character. Nine weights from Thin to Black each come with a matching italic, giving the family genuine range across display, branding and headline work. Its width is the defining trait: this is a typeface designed to occupy space rather than slip into it.
foundry_blurb: Albert is wide and entirely aware of it. Its broad, chunky forms take clear cues from Eurostile's retro confidence, then evolve into something more curvaceous and contemporary. Even in the lighter weights it holds presence – a relaxed but unmistakable display companion.

name: Jane
classification_notes: Modern American gothic grotesque drawing directly from Franklin Gothic and News Gothic. Three widths (standard, semicondensed, condensed), each in nine weights with matching italics. Retains the sturdy stroke weight and disciplined proportions of mid-century US grotesques while updating details for contemporary use. Latin and Cyrillic coverage throughout.
summary: A contemporary gothic sans rooted in the American grotesque tradition, spanning three widths and nine weights with italics across Latin and Cyrillic.
description: Jane draws openly from Franklin Gothic and News Gothic, taking that sturdy American gothic lineage and refining it for present-day use. The family covers three widths – standard, semicondensed and condensed – each in nine weights with matching italics. It holds up in body copy and at display scale, with Cyrillic support added alongside Latin throughout.
foundry_blurb: Jane wears her influences openly – she comes from the American gothic tradition of Franklin Gothic and News Gothic, and has evolved from there rather than broken away. The family spans three widths and a broad weight range, performing equally in running text and at large display sizes, with Cyrillic coverage alongside Latin.

name: George
classification_notes: Extreme-range variable grotesque with continuous weight and width axes. The wide end is imposing and ultra-heavy; the compressed end is sharp and alert. Anthropomorphic naming convention consistent with MNKY Type's broader library. No retail sale – licensed case by case.
summary: A brutalist variable grotesque spanning ultra-wide black to razor-thin compressed, built for high-impact display and identity work.
description: George runs a continuous variable axis from imposing, ultra-heavy wide forms to sharp, ultra-compressed styles, giving designers an extreme range within a single file. Its brutalist sensibility is consistent across the full span – nothing about it is soft or accommodating. Used by Collins for the Peloton identity, it performs at the level of demanding brand and editorial work.
foundry_blurb: George has an extreme range of styles: at one end, an ultra-heavy, wide form carrying its brutalist heritage; at the other, a sharp, compressed cut that's alert and ready to pounce. Won't beat you up – but it might try. Available by licence only; enquiries via the foundry direct.

name: Marcel
classification_notes: A grotesque sitting between geometric precision and classical grotesque tradition. Forms are sturdy and opinionated rather than neutral, with a distinct personality that holds across the full weight range. Not a humanist grotesque – more architectural and wilful, with enough alternates to adapt across contexts without losing character.
summary: An opinionated grotesque from MNKY Type that sits between geometric rigidity and classical warmth, with eight weights, matching italics and a set of alternates that have earned it placement in The New York Times Magazine.
description: Marcel occupies the territory between geometric precision and classic grotesque tradition, with sturdy, uncompromising forms that hold their character at any scale. Eight weights run from Extralight to Black, each with a matching italic, and a range of OpenType alternates extends its versatility without softening its personality. It has been used in The New York Times Magazine and Undercurrent, where its controlled confidence reads well under the demands of editorial work.
foundry_blurb: Marcel moves between geometry and the classic grotesque tradition, with a stubborn nature that comes through in every weight. From Thin to Black, the shapes are sure of themselves and uncompromising, while a range of alternates ensures the face works across a wide variety of contexts.

name: Maurice
classification_notes: Strict geometric sans-serif built on a pure grid, square proportions, minimal optical correction. Design intention described as brutalist but approachable – hard geometry softened by considered stylistic alternates and balanced spacing. No humanist compromise in the skeleton; warmth comes from detailing rather than form.
summary: A pure geometric sans-serif with nine weights, matching italics and Cyrillic coverage, whose strict grid-driven construction is tempered by a suite of stylistic alternates and a deliberately approachable texture.
description: Maurice is built on an uncompromising geometric skeleton – square proportions, maximum order, no optical fudging – yet reads as warm rather than cold, with its brutalist instincts offset by careful spacing and a broad set of stylistic alternates. Nine weights from Thin to Black each pair with a true italic, giving the family real range across text and display applications. Latin and Cyrillic coverage extends its reach into multilingual European work.
foundry_blurb: MNKY Type describes Maurice as a typeface with an obsessive love of pure geometry that comes first before all else. The result tips into brutalism, but always with a wink – so that what looks strict on close inspection ends up feeling approachable and warm. MNKY Type is an independent foundry split between New York and Chamonix, France, that donates a portion of proceeds to animal sanctuaries.

name: Louie
classification_notes: A grotesk-structured typeface with fully inverted stroke contrast – horizontals outweigh verticals, reversing the conventional stress pattern. The inversion is the defining and sole design idea. Available only in Regular and Regular Italic, limiting practical use to short-run display and headline contexts. Sits within MNKY Type's character-named, personality-driven library.
summary: Louie is a reversed-contrast grotesk from MNKY Type that flips conventional stroke weight so horizontals dominate – arresting for headlines, but a one-idea typeface with a very limited family.
description: Louie inverts the standard grotesk contrast: horizontal strokes are heavy, verticals thin – the opposite of how type conventionally works. It is available in Regular and Italic only, making no claim to range or versatility. The concept is clear and the execution is clean, but its appeal is narrow and entirely dependent on the visual novelty of that reversal.
foundry_blurb: Monkey Type describes Louie as a character who has just woken up, still with his contrast reversed and longing for the banana he was dreaming of – a wry nod to both the typeface's defining design quirk and the foundry's simian identity.

name: Koko
classification_notes: Draws formal ancestry from transitional serif models – Times New Roman and Plantin – but replaces their bracketed, tapered serifs with squared, blunt terminals. High contrast stems, upright structure, and a humanist underlying rhythm give it editorial authority. Five weights plus matching italics; no optical sizes or condensed cuts.
summary: Koko is a slab serif that applies squared, blunt terminals to the proportions and editorial authority of Times New Roman and Plantin.
description: Koko takes the framework of classic newspaper typefaces – high contrast, sturdy stems, upright rhythm – and replaces their tapered bracketed serifs with squared, almost blunt terminals. The result sits between the broadsheet tradition and something more architectural: grounded rather than delicate, assured rather than decorative. Five weights with matching italics make it usable across body copy and display settings in print-first editorial work.
foundry_blurb: Koko is steeped in the broadsheet tradition, drawing from the editorial authority of Times New Roman and Plantin. She updates those models with squared slab serifs and sturdy stems, steady in italic and built to hold the page.

name: Wilson
classification_notes: Subtly condensed humanist grotesque with a warm, approachable character. Nine weights with true italics give it real functional depth. Proportions sit slightly narrower than neutral without feeling compressed. Latin and Cyrillic coverage included.
summary: Wilson is a subtly condensed humanist grotesque from Monkey Type with nine weights, true italics and Latin and Cyrillic support – a friendly, versatile workhorse with genuine range.
description: Wilson sits in humanist grotesque territory with proportions tuned slightly narrower than neutral, giving it a quiet efficiency without feeling compressed. Nine weights from Thin to Black, each with a matching italic, make it genuinely useful across branding, editorial and screen contexts. Cyrillic support alongside Latin extends its reach into multilingual projects.
foundry_blurb: Monkey Type positions Wilson as a laid-back but current typeface – polite enough to work quietly in a supporting role, confident enough to hold its own when foregrounded. They describe it as comfortable across a wide variety of contexts, equally at ease blending into the background as it is taking centre stage.

name: Klaus
classification_notes: Rationalist grotesque with geometric influences. Slightly wide proportions, low contrast and orthogonal terminals. Designed for large-setting display use; avoids the narrower proportions of more utilitarian grotesques.
summary: A slightly wide rationalist grotesque from MNKY Type, balancing classic grotesque and geometric with low contrast and orthogonal terminals, suited to generous large-scale settings.
description: Klaus occupies a deliberate position between classic grotesque and geometric, its slightly wide proportions lending a grounded, unhurried character. Low contrast and orthogonal terminals keep it disciplined across nine weights from Thin to Black. A variable version alongside 18 static styles makes it adaptable for display and editorial work where spacing can breathe.
foundry_blurb: Klaus sees itself as a rationalist, balancing between classic grotesque and geometric with low contrast and orthogonal terminals. Slightly wide letterforms mean it works best given room to breathe, making it a natural companion in large settings.

name: Caesar
classification_notes: Humanist sans-serif with an unusually sharp, formal character — lean letterforms positioned closer to classical proportions than the warmer tradition typical of the genre. Released as a variable font with continuous weight (Thin to Black) and slant axes.
summary: A sharp, aristocratic humanist sans from MNKY Type, with lean, self-assured letterforms that carry unusual formality for the genre.
description: Caesar is a variable humanist sans spanning nine weights from Thin to Black, each with a matched italic and a continuous slant axis. The letterforms are precise and deliberately formal, carrying a regal quality that sets it apart from warmer, more approachable strands of humanist sans tradition. Full Latin and Cyrillic coverage extends its reach into multilingual editorial and identity work.
foundry_blurb: MNKY Type positions Caesar as sleek and classy, with sharp, confident shapes that reflect what they call a regal nature. Elegant and sophisticated, it carries an aristocratic demeanour — restrained authority rather than overt display.
